postgres.from:
The `pendingmagiclinks` collection:

| Field        | Notes                                                                         |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `email`      | Lowercased address the link was mailed to                                     |
| `tokenHash`  | sha256 of the token, hex, unique. The token itself is mailed and never stored |
| `expiresAt`  | When the link stops working                                                   |
| `consumedAt` | Set by the request that spends the link, `null` before that                   |
| `requestIp`  | Address the request came from                                                 |
| `userAgent`  | Agent string of the request                                                   |

A TTL index removes each record an hour after it expires. The delay is deliberate: the per-address hourly cap counts records created in the last hour, so they have to outlive the link.

Spending a link is a single `findOneAndUpdate` on `{ tokenHash, consumedAt: null }`. Two requests carrying the same token cannot both win it.
postgres.to:
The `pending_magic_links` table:

| Column        | Notes                                                                         |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `email`       | Lowercased address the link was mailed to                                     |
| `token_hash`  | sha256 of the token, hex, unique. The token itself is mailed and never stored |
| `expires_at`  | When the link stops working                                                   |
| `consumed_at` | Set by the request that spends the link, null before that                     |
| `request_ip`  | Address the request came from                                                 |
| `user_agent`  | Agent string of the request                                                   |

The retention job removes each row an hour after it expires. The delay is deliberate: the per-address hourly cap counts rows created in the last hour, so they have to outlive the link. A row that is still stored is not a link that still works: every read checks `expires_at`.

Spending a link is a single `UPDATE` of the row with that `token_hash` whose `consumed_at` is null. Two requests carrying the same token cannot both win it.

postgres.from:
On the user document, under `twoFactor`:

| Field           | Notes                                                              |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `enabled`       | `true` only after a first correct code                             |
| `secret`        | `{ ciphertext, iv, tag }`, AES-256-GCM under `TOTP_ENCRYPTION_KEY` |
| `confirmedAt`   | When the factor was turned on, `null` while a secret is pending    |
| `recoveryCodes` | `{ hash, usedAt }` per code, sha256 hex                            |
| `lastUsedStep`  | Highest TOTP step already spent                                    |

It is a new optional subdocument, so no migration is needed. Accounts written before it existed read back with the defaults, and `enabled` is `false` until someone runs setup.

`lastUsedStep` is what stops a replay. A code is good for 30 seconds and the check accepts one step either side, so without it, someone who reads a code off a screen has a window to use it again. Every accepted code records its step, and a step at or below the last one is refused.

The `twofactorchallenges` collection holds one record per half-finished sign-in:

| Field       | Notes                                            |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `user`      | Account the sign-in belongs to                   |
| `nonceHash` | sha256 of the nonce inside the cookie, unique    |
| `attempts`  | Wrong codes so far, capped at five               |
| `expiresAt` | Five minutes after the sign-in, with a TTL index |
postgres.to:
One row per account in `user_two_factor`:

| Column                                          | Notes                                                           |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`                                       | True only after a first correct code                            |
| `secret_ciphertext`, `secret_iv`, `secret_tag`  | The secret, AES-256-GCM under `TOTP_ENCRYPTION_KEY`             |
| `confirmed_at`                                  | When the factor was turned on, null while a secret is pending   |
| `last_used_step`                                | Highest TOTP step already spent                                 |

The recovery codes are one row each in `user_recovery_codes`, with the sha256 of the code in `hash` and `used_at` set when it is spent. Migration `0008_two_factor.sql` creates all three tables of this page. An account without a row has no second factor until someone runs setup.

`last_used_step` is what stops a replay. A code is good for 30 seconds and the check accepts one step either side, so without it, someone who reads a code off a screen has a window to use it again. Every accepted code records its step, and a step at or below the last one is refused.

The `two_factor_challenges` table holds one row per half-finished sign-in:

| Column       | Notes                                         |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `user_id`    | Account the sign-in belongs to                |
| `nonce_hash` | sha256 of the nonce inside the cookie, unique |
| `attempts`   | Wrong codes so far, capped at five            |
| `expires_at` | Five minutes after the sign-in                |

Every use compares `expires_at`, and the retention job removes the rows that lapsed.

MongoDB data persists in a named volume (`mongo-data`):

```bash
# List volumes
docker volume ls

# Inspect volume
docker volume inspect authstack-starter_mongo-data

# Backup volume
docker run --rm -v authstack-starter_mongo-data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/mongo-backup.tar.gz /data

# Restore volume
docker run --rm -v authstack-starter_mongo-data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar xzf /backup/mongo-backup.tar.gz -C /
```
postgres.to:
PostgreSQL data persists in a named volume (`postgres-data`):

```bash
# List volumes
docker volume ls

# Inspect volume
docker volume inspect authstack-starter_postgres-data

# Back up the database. The service keeps running: pg_dump reads one consistent state.
docker compose exec -T postgres sh -c 'pg_dump --username "$POSTGRES_USER" --format custom "$POSTGRES_DB"' > postgres-backup.dump

# Restore the database, with the backend stopped
docker compose stop backend
docker compose exec -T postgres sh -c 'pg_restore --username "$POSTGRES_USER" --dbname "$POSTGRES_DB" --clean --if-exists' < postgres-backup.dump
docker compose start backend
```

Do not copy the files of the volume while the service runs. A copy taken in the middle of a write may not start.
